title: The body, and saying what hurts
intro: Read plate 3 alongside this unit. Spanish uses the article where English uses a possessive — me lavo las manos, not mis manos — because the reflexive already tells you whose they are.

ex.es: Después de la carrera me dolía todo el cuerpo.
ex.en: After the race my whole body ached.

entries.note: de cabeza means upside down or headfirst.

ex.es: Cuidado, no te golpees la cabeza.
ex.en: Careful, don't bang your head.

entries.note: ¡Qué cara! means what a nerve — the same jump English makes with cheek.

ex.es: Se lavó la cara con agua fría.
ex.en: He washed his face with cold water.

ex.es: Tiene mucha cara para pedir eso.
ex.en: He's got some nerve asking for that.

entries.note: ¡Ojo! on its own is a warning: watch out.

ex.es: Cierra los ojos un momento.
ex.en: Close your eyes for a moment.

ex.es: Habló con la boca llena.
ex.en: He spoke with his mouth full.

entries.note: Ends in -o and is feminine anyway: la mano derecha, las manos limpias. One of the few genuine exceptions.

ex.es: Dame la mano para cruzar.
ex.en: Give me your hand to cross.

ex.es: Se rompió el brazo jugando fútbol.
ex.en: He broke his arm playing football.

ex.es: Tengo las piernas cansadas de tanto caminar.
ex.en: My legs are tired from so much walking.

entries.note: a pie means on foot. Plural is pies, not pieses.

ex.es: Vamos a pie, está cerca.
ex.en: Let's walk, it's close.

ex.es: Nos vemos al pie de la escalera.
ex.en: Meet me at the bottom of the stairs.

entries.note: Singular for the whole head of hair. el cabello is the more formal word.

ex.es: Se cortó el pelo muy corto.
ex.en: She cut her hair very short.

entries.note: The back of an object is la parte de atrás. de espaldas means with one's back turned.

ex.es: Me duele la espalda de estar sentado.
ex.en: My back hurts from sitting.

entries.note: Also the affectionate address, like English love or sweetheart.

ex.es: El corazón le latía muy rápido.
ex.en: His heart was beating very fast.

entries.note: Built backwards from English: the body part is the subject. Me duele la cabeza is literally the head hurts to me. Plural parts take duelen.

ex.es: Me duele la garganta.
ex.en: My throat hurts.

ex.es: ¿Te duelen los pies?
ex.en: Do your feet hurt?

entries.note: Name the part with de: dolor de cabeza, dolor de estómago, dolor de muelas.

ex.es: Tengo un dolor de cabeza terrible.
ex.en: I have a terrible headache.

ex.es: Habló de su dolor con calma.
ex.en: She spoke about her grief calmly.

entries.note: Takes estar, because it is a state: está enfermo. With ser it would mean a permanent condition.

ex.es: Mi hija está enferma y no fue a la escuela.
ex.en: My daughter is ill and didn't go to school.

entries.note: You have fever rather than a fever: tener fiebre.

ex.es: Tiene fiebre desde anoche.
ex.en: He's had a fever since last night.

entries.note: The same word you raise a glass with — see salud in unit 5.

ex.es: Su salud ha mejorado mucho.
ex.en: His health has improved a lot.

entries.note: el doctor is also used, especially as a title of address.

ex.es: Deberías ver a un médico.
ex.en: You should see a doctor.

entries.note: For a specific drug, el medicamento or la pastilla is more precise.

ex.es: Tómate la medicina después de comer.
ex.en: Take your medicine after eating.

ex.es: Estudia medicina en la capital.
ex.en: She studies medicine in the capital.

entries.note: estar cansado is to feel tired; ser cansado describes something that tires you out.

ex.es: Estoy muy cansado, me voy a dormir.
ex.en: I'm very tired, I'm going to sleep.

ex.es: El viaje es largo y cansado.
ex.en: The journey is long and tiring.
